claims.claim: at Bear Brook, Maine, dissolved P stayed at or below 3 µg/L even in storms, while total P rose with particulate Al and Fe (abstract)
claims.note: Neither the article nor its abstract was read. A search-engine summary of the abstract says total Al, Fe and P rose with discharge in the December 2001 and February 2002 high-flow events and dissolved Fe stayed ≤ 0.9 µmol/L; it gave no dissolved-P figure. If the abstract gives P in µmol/L, '≤ 3 µg/L' is a conversion (0.1 µmol/L = 3.1 µg/L) to be shown as such.

claims.claim: total P to ~53 µg/L (treated) vs ~10 (reference) in high flows; dissolved P ≤ 3 µg/L even in storms (abstract)
claims.note: Not read. The research note (catchment_P_loads.md lines 56–57) gives the abstract's values as dissolved P ≤ 0.1 µmol/L and total P 1.7 µmol/L on the rising limb in treated West Bear, 'about 5×' reference East Bear: so ~53 µg/L is a unit conversion (1.7 × 30.97) and ~10 µg/L reference is project arithmetic (53 ÷ 5), not printed values. The table should say so ('≈ 10, from the stated 5× ratio').

claims.claim: particulate Al, Fe and P travel together in Maine storm flows (abstract)
claims.note: Not read; the search summary relays the authors' conclusion that particulate Al, Fe and P are chemically linked during transport at high discharge in the acidified (West Bear) and reference (East Bear) streams.
